column4: This is the section's explicit convergence: the command "say, have you seen" turns the opening stance of surah 107 toward water, and مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ names the flowing water whose giver no human hand can replace.
This is the section's explicit shelter scene: Mary and her son are lodged on a رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ, joining a place fit for settled life to flowing water.
The section explicitly uses وَمَن لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ of Talut's river to show that طعم can make water an object of tasting, so "feeding" the poor reaches the provision of drink.
The section explicitly links فَآوَىٰ to the shelter of 23:50: God finds an orphan and gives him refuge, establishing divine shelter as the model behind care for the vulnerable.
Water runs through valley channels, each according to its measure, and the flood carries foam while what benefits people remains; this realizes both the section's watercourse and its useful gift.
God sends water, gives it to people to drink, and says they are not its keepers; that directly sharpens the section's charge against a hand that blocks water it did not originate or possess.
Measured water descends and is made to lodge in the earth, while God can take it away; the ayah supplies the section's descent, saturation, settlement, and dependence on the true giver.
Water from heaven becomes both human drink and vegetation in which livestock graze, exactly joining flowing provision to the pasture that lets a herd remain.
The question "do they not see" points to water driven into barren land, crops brought out, and both livestock and people eating, reproducing the section's whole water-to-food chain.
God sends water and brings forth diverse plants from it; this supplies the section's movement from water through earth to vegetation.
Eat and pasture your livestock states the two beneficiaries of the plants in 20:53, matching the section's food and abundant grazing ground.
The command that the human being look at his food begins a scene that traces food backward to poured water, just as the section hears water inside طَعَام.
The water is poured abundantly as the first material cause of the food named in 80:24; this makes explicit the section's claim that feeding reaches water.
The earth is split after the water is poured, giving the section's saturated ground the opening through which its provision grows.
Fruit and pasture are named together in the water-grown sequence, joining human food to the grazing ground central to the section's account of settled animals.
The sequence is declared provision for "you and your livestock," completing the same shared water-food-pasture economy developed by the section.
أَفَرَءَيْتُمُ ٱلْمَاءَ ٱلَّذِى تَشْرَبُونَ directs the "have you seen" stance toward drinking water, as the section says the opening question should be directed toward its final water image.
The question whether people sent the water down or God did identifies the source of the flow and exposes the absurdity of treating it as the withholder's own.
At Midian, people water their flocks while two women hold theirs back until the shepherds leave; access to water, herd movement, and an obstructed turn at the source meet in one concrete scene.
Moses waters the women's flock for them, reversing the blocked access of 28:23 and embodying the section's opposite of the hand that withholds a life-sustaining flow.
Have you not seen introduces rain conducted as springs through the earth and then varied crops; it directly supplies the hidden channels and watered growth behind the section's image.
God brings the earth's water and its pasture out of it, placing the two successive terms of the section's process in a single ayah.
The water and pasture of 79:31 are provision for people and their livestock, confirming why a well-watered grazing place permits settled life.
Pure rain revives dead country and gives drink to many humans and cattle; it joins restored land, watering, and herd provision as the section does.
Gardens are supplied by springs made to gush within them, a direct scene of water coursing through productive ground.
People eat the resulting fruit and are asked for gratitude in relation to what their hands did not produce; this supports the section's insistence that the withholder did not make the flow.

Homes are made سَكَنًا, while livestock hides make dwellings useful on the day of ظَعْن and the day of staying; this exactly unfolds the section's dictionary contrast between settled pasture and departure.
God makes the earth a place of settlement, قَرَارًا, and places rivers through it; this is a close nonlexical twin to the section's pairing of stable habitation and مَعِين.
مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ is the very dictionary wording invoked by the section, identifying habitual obstruction of good as the human character behind blocking the channel.
The repeated description مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ supplies the same habitual-withholder sense cited in the section and makes the withheld small benefit part of a settled moral type.
When good touches the anxious human he is مَنُوعًا, a withholding form from the same root; the ayah locates the blocked flow in the possessor's response to received good.
In the same surah as 67:30, the question asks who could provide if God withheld His provision; it distinguishes God's decisive control of supply from a human's blameworthy refusal to pass it on.
A cup from مَعِين is passed around in the Garden; it preserves the section's dictionary sense of accessible flowing water while showing it freely circulated as drink.
Cups, ewers, and a cup from مَعِين present flowing water in vessels and in circulation, a direct lexical development of the section's final word as water rather than merely an object of aid.
وَلَا تَحَٰٓضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ nearly repeats 107:3 in the plural, confirming that failure even to urge the poor person's feeding is the social stoppage the water image exposes.
The condemned person does not urge طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ, the same formulation as 107:3; beside this section it makes withholding drink part of the same failure to sustain the poor.
The people of the Fire confess that they did not feed the poor; this states as an omitted act what the section expands from food into water and settled subsistence.

Those told to spend from God's provision refuse by asking why they should feed someone God could feed; the ayah exposes exactly the false inference the image rejects—divine provision does not excuse a human block in its passage.

Sincere spending is pictured as a garden on a رَبْوَة struck by rain and yielding double produce; water, high ground, fruit, and generous release form the positive counterpart to the withholding hand.

God makes twelve springs burst from the rock, each people knows its drinking place, and all are told to eat and drink from God's provision; flowing water is apportioned for communal access rather than blocked.

The parallel Moses scene makes twelve springs issue, assigns each community its drinking place, and couples water with God's food provision, concretely linking water, settlement, and shared sustenance.
In the other Qur'anic scene of Mary, she is told not to grieve because God has placed a سَرِيّ beneath her, commonly understood here as a stream; it supplies water at her place of refuge.
Mary is told to eat, drink, and be comforted after the stream and dates are provided, joining shelter to the two forms of sustenance that the section holds together.
The water is declared a share divided among the people and the she-camel, with each turn attended; this makes access to water a divinely set right rather than a benefit one party may obstruct.
The she-camel has a drinking share and the people a share on a known day, another concrete boundary governing access to the common water on which herds and humans depend.
The brothers say مُنِعَ مِنَّا ٱلْكَيْلُ, that their food measure will be withheld; the same root is thus used for stopping essential provision, clarifying the force of withholding al-māʿūn.

After naming productive gardens and crops, the ayah commands giving their due at harvest; it carries water-grown abundance into an enforceable human share, the opposite of arresting its benefit at one's hand.
The garden owners conspire that no poor person shall enter upon them that day; their attempt to stop produce before it reaches the poor is the agricultural form of the section's blocked channel.
A garden's water may become غَوْرًا and impossible to retrieve; this is the explicit reverse of accessible flowing مَعِين and illuminates what is at stake when 67:30 asks who can restore it.
God could make the drinking water bitter; this boundary to 56:68-69 shows that drinkability itself is given, deepening the blame of withholding usable water without gratitude.

Abraham settles his descendants in an uncultivated valley and asks that they receive fruits; unlike the naturally watered pasture of the section, their staying depends visibly on God's provision and human gratitude.

Showy spending is soil on rock stripped bare by a downpour; water produces no lasting benefit where giving is performance, a pointed reversal of the section's water that enters earth and sustains others.
Garden fruit is neither cut off nor مَمْنُوعَةٍ; unwithheld abundance gives the lexical and material opposite of the hand that prevents a small necessary benefit.
Good land yields vegetation by its Lord's leave, whereas bad land yields only scant growth; the contrast shows that receiving the same water is not identical with passing on its benefit.
A flowing spring, عَيْنٌ جَارِيَةٌ, states without the root م ع ن the exact dictionary gloss the section gives for مَعِين.
Two springs flow in the two gardens; عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ provides a direct nonlexical formulation of the running-water scene.
Two gushing springs offer a more forceful form of accessible water, extending the section's concern with an unobstructed source.
God's servants drink from a spring and cause it to gush abundantly, presenting water as a gift whose course is opened and shared.
A river is made to gush between two fruitful gardens, joining a watercourse through land to sustained produce.
The rhetorical question asks who sent water down and grew splendid gardens that humans could not grow, directing attention from the result to the giver just as the section does.
Pure water is sent from heaven; 25:49 then states its effects on dead land, animals, and people, so this row contributes the source and quality of the flow.
The water has been distributed among people so that they remember, yet most respond with ingratitude; distribution and refusal add a moral frame to the provision described in 25:48-49.
Every living thing is made from water, grounding the section's more specific chain from water to grass, herd, and human food in water's general life-giving role.
Steadfastness is answered with abundant water, making plentiful water a supplied condition of flourishing rather than a human possession.
The abundant water of 72:16 is also a test; that qualification parallels the river test in 2:249 and turns received provision into a measure of conduct.
Rain mingles with the earth's vegetation from which people and cattle eat, closely matching the section's chain from descending water to shared pasture and food.
Water from heaven brings forth the growth of all things, including green growth, grain, and fruit; it elaborates what the section compresses into earth drinking and pasture emerging.
Heavy clouds are driven to dead land, water descends, and fruits come forth; the ayah presents the same directed movement from source to receptive earth and produce.
Blessed water grows gardens and harvested grain, directly joining received water to food that can pass to people.
The growth in 50:9-10 is provision for servants and revival of dead land, naming both recipient and effect of the watered earth.
Abundant pouring water descends from rain clouds, supplying the first stage of the section's downward-moving flow.
Grain and vegetation are brought out by that water, giving the next stage of the section's water-to-food movement.
Dense gardens complete the result of the poured water in 78:14, a settled landscape made productive by the flow.
God sends water from the sky and brings out fruits as provision, so the food a person might withhold is first identified as divine supply.
Rain produces fruits as provision and rivers are subjected for people, bringing the source, edible result, and ongoing watercourse into one divine gift.
The water of 16:10 grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit; it develops the human-food side of the same water that creates pasture.
Grain is the first named crop from the watered and split earth, making the food in 80:24 a concrete result rather than an isolated commodity.
Grapes and fodder continue the water-grown sequence and bring human produce beside animal feed.
Olives and palms extend the produce issuing from the watered earth and destined for use.
Thick gardens form the productive habitat between poured water and the fruit and pasture of 80:31.
The dead earth is revived and grain brought from it for people to eat; 36:34 supplies the gardens and springs that make this food-chain connection explicit.
Mary is told to shake the palm so fresh dates fall to her; between the stream in 19:24 and eating and drinking in 19:26, the act shows supplied shelter becoming food in hand.
Feeding on a day of hunger presents food as the released benefit in precisely the condition where withholding it is most consequential.
The first recipient of that feeding is an orphan relative, linking sustenance to the vulnerable person whom 93:6 says God sheltered.
The other recipient is a poor person in misery, completing a concrete alternative to refusing طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ.
The righteous give food they value to the poor, orphan, and captive; the food visibly passes through their hands instead of stopping there.
A recognized right belongs in their wealth to the asker and deprived, making the received good a channel with a due outlet rather than unrestricted private control.
Immediately after the portrait of the human as withholding in 70:21, the people of prayer have a known right in their wealth, offering the section's positive alternative.
That known right is for the asker and deprived, identifying the outlet through which received good must move.
God extends His gift to both groups and His gift is not restricted; the unrestricted divine giving forms a thematic boundary against a human hand that arrests benefit.
The miserly both urge miserliness and conceal what God gave them from His bounty, closely matching the section's person who treats a received flow as something to stop.
Those who hoard what God gave from His bounty mistake the withholding for good; the ayah reinforces the section's distinction between receiving provision and owning its source.
The command to lodge vulnerable women where the addressees dwell makes سكن an obligation to extend shelter, complementing the section's link between settlement and care.
God brings out the pasture; although water is unstated here, the ayah isolates the grazing ground that the section treats as the outcome of water and the cause of a herd's staying.
Water descends in measure and revives dead land, joining measured supply to receptive earth in the same causal relation as the section.
Have you not seen rain descend and the earth become green; the stance of seeing and the ground's response both echo the section's directed question about water.

The fasting compensation of طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ uses the section's two named words for a concrete due owed to a poor person; the section's dictionary extension asks the reader to hear drink within that subsistence.
Rain revives the earth after death and living creatures are dispersed through it; this supplies both the watered ground and the animal life sustained by its growth.
Asked who sends water from heaven and revives dead earth, the addressees must answer "God"; this is a direct parallel to the section's question about who brings flowing water.
Abraham identifies God as the one who feeds him and gives him drink, joining the section's two forms of sustenance at their true source.
Have you seen what you sow? extends the same seeing-question used for water in 56:68 to the crop produced after water enters the earth.
The question whether humans make the sowing grow or God does prevents the recipient from claiming authorship of the pasture or food that later passes through human hands.
Lofty mountains and fresh water given to drink bring height and potable water together, closely paralleling the high, well-watered refuge of 23:50.

The hypocrites propose stopping expenditure on the Prophet's companions until they disperse, while God's are the treasuries of heaven and earth; withheld provision here is explicitly intended to force departure, the reverse of abundant pasture permitting a group to stay.
The hypocrites "close their hands," giving the section's withholding hand an exact ethical gesture and showing refusal to let received good pass onward.

A town secure and at ease receives abundant provision from every place, then ingratitude turns that condition into hunger and fear; settlement and food are thus joined, with their loss marking the boundary.
People of bounty are told not to swear off giving relatives, the poor, and emigrants; the ayah directly reverses an attempted blockage of benefit by a hand that has itself received bounty.

The earth is commanded to swallow its water, the sky to stop, and the flood subsides; this divine closing of the water's course marks the boundary between providential control and a human's blameworthy obstruction.
A thirsty person takes a mirage for water but finds none on arrival; inaccessible, illusory water is a precise reversal of the available مَعِين developed by the section.
The people of the Fire drink from a boiling spring, reversing the beneficial flowing spring of 88:12 and showing that the mere presence of flowing drink does not make it merciful provision.
Life in the Garden is defined by neither hunger nor nakedness, setting a boundary in which settled shelter includes reliable food and covering.
The Garden also excludes thirst and exposure to the sun, completing the link between habitation, drink, and protection that the section finds in a well-watered refuge.
Ruined settlements are pictured beside an abandoned well; the conjunction of a lost water source and emptied habitation reverses the section's flowing water that enables staying.

Whatever mercy God opens none can withhold, and whatever He withholds none can release; this establishes the theological boundary behind the section's human attempt to dam a gift whose source he does not control.

Against the charge that God's hand is fettered, the ayah says His hands are outspread and He gives as He wills; open divine giving supplies the direct contrary to the section's closed, withholding hand.
The command not to keep one's hand chained to one's neck gives the withholding disposition a bodily image closely matching the hand that blocks the section's channel.
Whoever is miserly is miserly only against himself, while God is rich and humans are needy; the ayah exposes the dependence of the person who tries to arrest a received benefit.
Following the dwellings of 16:80, God provides shade and mountain shelters; it continues the concrete account of what makes a place habitable and protective.
The Children of Israel are lodged in a sound settlement and provided good things, pairing dwelling with supplied sustenance as the section pairs قرار with water.
A secure sanctuary receives fruits gathered from every kind as provision from God, linking stable habitation to food brought into it.
Feeding against hunger and granting security against fear place subsistence and settled safety together, an indirect parallel to food, water, and refuge in the section.
Abraham asks that the town be secure and that its people receive fruits, joining a stable place to supplied food in the same relation as the section's watered shelter.
The people are asked whether they expect to remain secure among gardens and springs, directly linking settled security to abundant water.
Crops and palms complete the gardens-and-springs setting of 26:147, showing the edible growth that makes such staying possible.
Livestock are beautiful when brought home and when sent out to pasture, a concrete picture of the herd's movement between its settled place and grazing ground.
Water makes the humbled earth stir and swell, another direct formulation of ground receiving water and becoming productive.
Water descends from the sky and revives the earth after death, repeating the causal movement on which the section's pasture scene depends.
Water sent from heaven causes every noble kind of growth, supplying the vegetation stage of the section's watercourse.
Water from heaven mingles with earth's vegetation before it becomes dry fragments; the ayah traces the same water-to-growth process while exposing its temporal limit.
The promised Garden contains rivers of water that does not spoil, presenting an enduring, unobstructed flow as the positive boundary to water that sinks or is withheld.
Job is given a cool spring for washing and drinking, showing accessible water as God's restorative provision for both body and thirst.
Feeding ten poor people as expiation makes the section's named food and poor recipients a concrete, measured obligation rather than optional surplus.
Feeding sixty poor people is required when the other expiation is impossible, another legal setting in which sustenance must reach the poor.
Believers are told to spend from good earnings and from what God brings out of the earth, carrying water-grown produce onward as human giving.
The one who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient embodies the inward claim behind blocking a provision whose source remains God.
Towns exulting in their livelihood become dwellings scarcely inhabited afterward; lost provision and lost settlement together reverse the section's nourishing water that permits continued residence.
